title: Control and Coordination
seo_title: Control and Coordination Class 10 Science Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 6)
standard_text: Control and co-ordination in animals and plants: tropic movements in plants; introduction of plant hormones; control and co-ordination in animals: nervous system; voluntary, involuntary and reflex action; chemical co-ordination: animal hormones.
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 10 Science worksheets for NCERT Chapter 6: neurons, reflex arcs, parts of the brain, plant hormones and tropisms, and human hormones and glands. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Nerves give fast messages; hormones give slow, lasting ones.
key_sub: Reflex: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector.
body_html:
How to think about it

In animals, receptors detect stimuli and neurons carry electrical impulses to the brain or spinal cord, which send messages to effectors (muscles and glands). Reflex actions are quick and controlled by the spinal cord. The cerebrum handles thinking, the cerebellum balance, and the medulla involuntary actions.

Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood: insulin lowers blood sugar, thyroxine controls metabolism, adrenaline prepares for emergencies. Plants respond by growth (tropisms) controlled by hormones such as auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid.

Example

A shoot bends to light. Which hormone?

auxin moves to the shaded side

Answer: auxin

Example

Which gland makes insulin?

it controls blood sugar

Answer: the pancreas

Common mistakes

  • Thinking reflex actions are controlled by the cerebrum.
  • Mixing up phototropism and geotropism.
  • Saying hormones travel along nerves.

faq.q: How do plants respond without a nervous system?
faq.a: By hormones that change growth (tropisms) and by quick changes of water in cells, as in the touch-me-not plant.

faq.q: Why is the spinal cord important in reflex actions?
faq.a: It processes the message quickly and sends a response without waiting for the brain.

items.q: Which part does this job: containing the nucleus of the neuron?
items.e: The cell body: containing the nucleus of the neuron.

items.q: Which part of the brain is the main thinking part?
items.e: It has areas for sensing, thinking and movement.

items.q: What are involuntary actions?
c: actions not under our conscious control, such as heartbeat and breathing
items.e: They are controlled by the medulla.

items.q: What is the job of effectors (muscles and glands)?
c: picking up the message at the nerve ending
containing the nucleus of the neuron
carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body
items.e: Effectors (muscles and glands): responding to the message.

items.q: Which part of the brain controls walking in a straight line?
items.e: It coordinates balance and posture.

items.q: Why do roots grow downwards?
c: they are pushed by the stem
they are positively geotropic (they respond to gravity)
items.e: Shoots are negatively geotropic.

items.q: What happens at a synapse?
c: the impulse releases chemicals that start a new impulse in the next neuron
items.e: This makes sure the message travels one way.

items.q: What is the job of the axon?
c: carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body
picking up the message at the nerve ending
the gap where a chemical passes the message to the next cell
containing the nucleus of the neuron
items.e: The axon: carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body.

items.q: Which part protects the brain?
items.e: The spinal cord is protected by the vertebral column.

items.q: Which hormone causes the heart to beat faster during fear?
items.e: It also sends more blood to the muscles.

items.q: Which gland is both endocrine and exocrine?
items.e: It secretes insulin and pancreatic juice.

items.q: How do tendrils of a pea plant wind round a support?
c: the side away from the support grows faster
the side touching the support grows faster
items.e: This is thigmotropism (response to touch).

items.q: What is the main difference between nervous and hormonal control?
c: nerves give fast, short responses; hormones give slower, longer-lasting ones
items.e: Both work together to coordinate the body.

items.q: What is the path of a reflex arc?
c: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay) → motor neuron → effector
items.e: The brain is informed but not needed for the response.

items.q: Which part does this job: picking up the message at the nerve ending?
items.e: Dendrites: picking up the message at the nerve ending.

items.q: Which part does this job: detecting a stimulus, for example in the skin or tongue?
items.e: Receptors: detecting a stimulus, for example in the skin or tongue.

items.q: Which part does this job: responding to the message?
items.e: Effectors (muscles and glands): responding to the message.

items.q: What is the job of dendrites?
c: picking up the message at the nerve ending
carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body
the gap where a chemical passes the message to the next cell
containing the nucleus of the neuron
items.e: Dendrites: picking up the message at the nerve ending.

items.q: Which part does this job: carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body?
items.e: The axon: carrying the electrical impulse away from the cell body.

items.q: What is the job of the cell body?
c: the gap where a chemical passes the message to the next cell
picking up the message at the nerve ending
containing the nucleus of the neuron
items.e: The cell body: containing the nucleus of the neuron.

items.q: What is the job of the cerebellum (hindbrain)?
c: some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes
involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting
balance, posture and precise voluntary movements
items.e: The cerebellum (hindbrain): balance, posture and precise voluntary movements.

items.q: Why do nervous messages work faster than hormones?
c: they travel as electrical impulses along neurons
nerves are thicker than blood vessels
items.e: Hormones travel in the blood.

items.q: What happens to the pupil of the eye in bright light?
items.e: This is a reflex that protects the retina.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones?
items.e: The hypothalamus: controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones.

items.q: How does the pollen tube find the ovule?
c: it grows towards chemicals from the ovule (chemotropism)
items.e: This is a directional growth response.

items.q: What is the job of the hypothalamus?
c: controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones
items.e: The hypothalamus: controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones.

items.q: Why is iodised salt recommended?
c: iodine is needed to make thyroxine and prevent goitre
items.e: Thyroxine controls metabolism.

items.q: What is the job of the midbrain?
c: some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes
controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones
items.e: The midbrain: some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting?
items.e: The medulla (hindbrain): involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

items.q: What is the job of cerebrospinal fluid?
c: balance, posture and precise voluntary movements
carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions
items.e: Cerebrospinal fluid: cushioning the brain against shocks.

items.q: What is the job of the medulla (hindbrain)?
c: involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting
items.e: The medulla (hindbrain): involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

items.q: What is the growth response of a plant part to water called?
items.e: Water: hydrotropism.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: protecting the brain?
items.e: The cranium (skull): protecting the brain.

items.q: What is the growth response of a plant part to light called?
items.e: Light: phototropism.

items.q: What is the job of the spinal cord?
c: involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting
carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions
some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes
items.e: The spinal cord: carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions.

items.q: Which stimulus causes geotropism?
c: touch (such as a tendril around a support)
items.e: Gravity: geotropism.

items.q: What is the advantage of a feedback mechanism in hormone control?
c: it keeps the amount of hormone at the right level
it makes more hormone all the time
items.e: For example, high blood sugar triggers insulin release.

items.q: What is the job of the cranium (skull)?
c: involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting
items.e: The cranium (skull): protecting the brain.

items.q: What is the job of the cerebrum (forebrain)?
c: controlling the pituitary gland by releasing hormones
carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions
items.e: The cerebrum (forebrain): thinking, memory and voluntary actions.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: regulating breathing?
items.e: The pons: regulating breathing.

items.q: What is the role of the plant hormone abscisic acid?
c: inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves
promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot
items.e: Abscisic acid: inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves.

items.q: Which gland is called the master gland?
items.e: It controls many other glands.

items.q: Which stimulus causes hydrotropism?
c: chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule)
items.e: Water: hydrotropism.

items.q: Why does a growing shoot bend away from gravity?
items.e: Roots are positively geotropic.

items.q: What is the role of the plant hormone auxin?
c: promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot
inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves
items.e: Auxin: promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot.

items.q: What is the growth response of a plant part to chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule) called?
items.e: Chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule): chemotropism.

items.q: What is the role of the plant hormone cytokinins?
c: promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot
inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves
items.e: Cytokinins: promoting cell division.

items.q: What is the growth response of a plant part to gravity called?
items.e: Gravity: geotropism.

items.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light?
c: auxin collects on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer
auxin is made in the roots
items.e: This is positive phototropism.

items.q: Why is blood sugar kept within a narrow range?
c: the body needs a steady supply of glucose; too much or too little is harmful
sugar is stored in the brain
items.e: Insulin brings it down when it rises.

items.q: What is the function of the motor neuron in a reflex arc?
c: carrying the message from the spinal cord to the effector
carrying the message to the brain only
items.e: The effector is a muscle or gland.

items.q: Why does a touch-me-not plant fold its leaves when touched?
c: cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them
items.e: This is not growth; it is quick movement.

items.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for promoting cell division?
items.e: Cytokinins: promoting cell division.

items.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves?
items.e: Abscisic acid: inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves.

items.q: What is the role of the plant hormone gibberellins?
c: promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot
inhibiting growth and causing wilting of leaves
items.e: Gibberellins: promoting growth of the stem.

items.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot?
items.e: Auxin: promoting cell elongation; it moves to the shaded side of a shoot.

items.q: Which stimulus causes chemotropism?
c: touch (such as a tendril around a support)
chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule)
items.e: Chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule): chemotropism.

items.q: Which stimulus causes thigmotropism?
c: chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule)
touch (such as a tendril around a support)
items.e: Touch (such as a tendril around a support): thigmotropism.

items.q: What is the function of the sensory neuron in a reflex arc?
c: carrying the message to the muscle
carrying the message from the receptor to the spinal cord
items.e: The motor neuron carries it to the effector.

items.q: Which stimulus causes phototropism?
c: touch (such as a tendril around a support)
chemicals (such as the pollen tube growing to the ovule)
items.e: Light: phototropism.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the pancreas?
items.e: The pancreas secretes insulin.

items.q: Which gland secretes adrenaline?
items.e: Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the thyroid gland?
items.e: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland?
items.e: The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone.

items.q: What is the main job of testosterone?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
regulating sleep and the daily body clock
items.e: Testosterone (the testes): changes in boys at puberty.

items.q: What is the main job of melatonin?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
regulating sleep and the daily body clock
items.e: Melatonin (the pineal gland): regulating sleep and the daily body clock.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the thymus?
items.e: The thymus secretes thymosin.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the testes?
items.e: The testes secretes testosterone.

items.q: What is the main job of growth hormone?
c: controlling the level of calcium in the blood
items.e: Growth hormone (the pituitary gland): controlling growth of the body.

items.q: Which gland secretes thymosin?
items.e: Thymosin is secreted by the thymus.

items.q: What is the main job of adrenaline?
c: preparing the body for action in an emergency
items.e: Adrenaline (the adrenal glands): preparing the body for action in an emergency.

items.q: What is the main job of releasing hormones?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
stimulating the pituitary to release hormones
items.e: Releasing hormones (the hypothalamus): stimulating the pituitary to release hormones.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the parathyroid glands?
items.e: The parathyroid glands secretes parathormone.

items.q: Which gland secretes oestrogen?
items.e: Oestrogen is secreted by the ovaries.

items.q: What is the main job of thymosin?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
stimulating the pituitary to release hormones
helping the immune system develop in children
items.e: Thymosin (the thymus): helping the immune system develop in children.

items.q: What is the main job of parathormone?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
controlling the level of calcium in the blood
items.e: Parathormone (the parathyroid glands): controlling the level of calcium in the blood.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the hypothalamus?
items.e: The hypothalamus secretes releasing hormones.

items.q: Which gland secretes parathormone?
items.e: Parathormone is secreted by the parathyroid glands.

items.q: Which gland secretes growth hormone?
items.e: Growth hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland.

items.q: What is the main job of thyroxine?
c: controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism
regulating sleep and the daily body clock
items.e: Thyroxine (the thyroid gland): controlling carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes?
items.e: The midbrain: some reflexes such as the movement of the eyes.

items.q: Which gland secretes testosterone?
items.e: Testosterone is secreted by the testes.

items.q: What is a reflex action?
c: a quick, automatic response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord
items.e: Pulling your hand from a hot object is a reflex.

items.q: Which gland secretes thyroxine?
items.e: Thyroxine is secreted by the thyroid gland.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: balance, posture and precise voluntary movements?
items.e: The cerebellum (hindbrain): balance, posture and precise voluntary movements.

items.q: What causes gigantism?
c: too little iodine for making thyroxine
too much growth hormone in childhood
too little growth hormone in childhood
items.e: Gigantism is caused by too much growth hormone in childhood.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: protecting the spinal cord?
items.e: The vertebral column: protecting the spinal cord.

items.q: What causes dwarfism?
c: too little growth hormone in childhood
too much growth hormone in childhood
too little iodine for making thyroxine
items.e: Dwarfism is caused by too little growth hormone in childhood.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: thinking, memory and voluntary actions?
items.e: The cerebrum (forebrain): thinking, memory and voluntary actions.

items.q: What is the job of the vertebral column?
c: carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions
items.e: The vertebral column: protecting the spinal cord.

items.q: What causes goitre (a swollen neck)?
c: too little growth hormone in childhood
too little iodine for making thyroxine
too much growth hormone in childhood
items.e: Goitre (a swollen neck) is caused by too little iodine for making thyroxine.

items.q: What causes diabetes?
c: too much growth hormone in childhood
too little iodine for making thyroxine
too little growth hormone in childhood
items.e: Diabetes is caused by too little insulin.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the ovaries?
items.e: The ovaries secretes oestrogen.

items.q: What is the job of the pons?
c: balance, posture and precise voluntary movements
items.e: The pons: regulating breathing.

items.q: Which hormone is secreted by the adrenal glands?
items.e: The adrenal glands secretes adrenaline.

items.q: Which part of the nervous system or its protection does this: carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions?
items.e: The spinal cord: carrying messages to and from the brain and controlling reflex actions.

items.q: What is a stimulus?
c: a change in the surroundings that an organism responds to
items.e: Light, heat and touch are stimuli.

items.q: Which gland secretes releasing hormones?
items.e: Releasing hormones is secreted by the hypothalamus.

items.q: What is the main job of oestrogen?
c: regulating sleep and the daily body clock
helping the immune system develop in children
items.e: Oestrogen (the ovaries): changes in girls at puberty.

items.q: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary muscles?
c: voluntary muscles move when we decide; involuntary muscles move on their own
voluntary muscles are only in the heart
involuntary muscles are only in the legs
items.e: Heart muscle is involuntary.
